summary: Presents theoretical and practical reasons to redesign the ARPANET communication protocols. It discusses multipacket messages, Host retransmission, duplicate detection, sequencing and acknowledgment, and proposes simplifications to the IMP-to-IMP protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 635 assesses ARPANET protocol performance and proposes shifting more reliability work from IMPs to hosts. Its ideas include host-level ordering and acknowledgments, simpler IMP forwarding and full-duplex connections, while leaving congestion control as an open issue.

subtitle: A proposal to simplify ARPANET protocols by moving reliability work to hosts.

tldr.problem: The author argues that message-at-a-time Host-to-Host operation limits throughput and that IMP reassembly and sequencing can create lockup risks.
tldr.mechanism: The paper proposes that hosts handle message ordering, retransmission, duplicate detection and end-to-end acknowledgment, allowing simpler IMP protocols and potentially removing multipacket reassembly.
tldr.outcome: RFC 635 presents an assessment and redesign proposals, while noting unresolved congestion and implementation questions.

today: RFC 635 is a 1974 assessment proposing changes to ARPANET host and IMP protocols; it also identifies unresolved questions, including congestion control.

sections.title: Why Reconsider the Protocols
sections.content:
After several years of ARPANET experience, the author argues that the Host-to-Host, IMP-to-IMP and Host/IMP protocols should be reconsidered. The paper reviews throughput and delay, message reassembly, retransmission, duplicate detection, sequencing and acknowledgment.

Its conclusions include removing multipacket messages if hosts can send enough single-packet messages, avoiding destination IMP ordering that can lead to lockup, and moving retransmission, error detection, duplicate detection and ordering to hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: The paper asks whether the network's protocols could be simpler and faster after several years of use. It proposes that hosts, rather than IMPs, take responsibility for more of the message-delivery work.

sections.title: Throughput and Lockup Risks
sections.content:
The paper says that although the IMP subnet could deliver up to 80 kb/sec between hosts, the current Host-to-Host protocol could not offer more than 40 kb/sec on a single connection under its analysis, and throughput falls with more IMP hops. The message-at-a-time design waits for an RFNM before sending the next message.

The author also reviews deadlock risks from multipacket reassembly and destination-IMP ordering. Buffers can be occupied by out-of-order messages while earlier messages wait to be delivered. A limit of four in-transit messages per destination reduced the probability of lockup but did not eliminate it.
sections.plainLanguage: The current protocol sends one message at a time on a connection, so longer paths make it wait more. Buffering and ordering at IMPs can also leave messages unable to move forward.

sections.title: Host-Level Reliability and Flow Control
sections.content:
The proposed division of work has hosts retransmit lost messages, detect duplicates, order incoming data and acknowledge delivery end to end. In that design, IMP reassembly and ordering could be removed, and the RFNM would no longer serve as the delivery acknowledgment.

The paper discusses a window-based flow-control proposal: a receiver indicates the sequence range the sender may transmit, and acknowledgments can be carried with data traveling in the reverse direction of a full-duplex connection. This could avoid a separate control connection, but congestion across the IMP subnet remains an unresolved issue.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts could track sequence numbers, resend missing data and confirm delivery. A receiver could also tell a sender how much data it may have in flight, with control information carried back alongside data.

sections.title: Other Proposed Simplifications and Open Issues
sections.content:
The paper suggests that multipacket reassembly may not be needed if hosts can keep enough single-packet messages in flight. It also considers full-duplex logical connections and carrying control information in message headers, rather than using a separate control connection.

The author notes that the network still needs a way to manage congestion when too much traffic reaches an IMP or destination. He presents monitoring throughput and adjusting transmission as possibilities and invites further discussion of protocol requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposals aim to simplify IMP work and use two-way connections for data and control. The paper leaves network congestion as a problem that still needs a solution.

references.text: Kahn, R. E. and W. Crowther, Flow Control in a Resource-Sharing Computer Network, June 1972.
